[[RunningHead]]

Call for papers: connecting in relation to Covid-19

Maria Papadima and Lydia Hartland-Rowe

Lydia Hartland-Rowe

Lydia Hartland-Rowe   lydia.hartlandrowe@childpsychotherapy.org.uk

Since early in 2020, our experience of living and working in the context of a global pandemic has preoccupied and changed us in ways that have felt both distressing and creative. One of the most extraordinary features has been the global nature of this experience, shared simultaneously across countries and cultures, both in the shape of the virus, and in some of our ‘virtual’ solutions and connections. For our next issue in the Journal of Child Psychotherapy (46.3) we want to focus on aspects of clinicians’ experience of 2020 so far, which will be presented and also connected through a commentary on emergent themes to inform our clinical and theoretical discourse.

We are looking for shorter pieces, 2000–3000 words, focusing on various areas of the experience, as it has developed so far. Possible topics could include: working with bereaved children, digital working, working remotely with colleagues, working in the transference remotely, maintaining psychotherapy with younger children online, working on the phone, dialogues between clinicians in different countries, living and working within a polarised environment, beginning work online and assessing … and anything else that you feel you would like to comment on. We encourage submissions from child psychotherapists and child analysts internationally.

The deadline for submissions is 1st January 2021. If you would like to discuss a possible submission please don't hesitate to contact Maria Papadima (maria.papadima@childpsychotherapy.org.uk) or Lydia Hartland-Rowe(lydia.hartlandrowe@childpsychotherapy.org.uk).

Under the Skin: a psychoanalytic film commentary

Rosemary Winter

Rosemary Winter

Sheffield

Rosemary Winter   rosemarywinter@gmail.com

The sci-fi/horror film Under the Skin (2013) is director Jonathan Glaser’s stripped back telling of the novel of the same title by Faber (2000). Its narrative is based on the emotionless Alien (Scarlett Johansson), whose primary function is to seduce lone men and lure them to a terrifying end. The Alien’s journey is one that develops, as she becomes increasingly cognisant of a physical and mental experience beyond the primary function of her task. This sets in motion a sequence of events that leads to her eventual and brutal murder.

I will discuss how the Alien functions as a mechanism for projective identification and acts as both the conduit of primitive terror, and how later in the film, the Alien becomes the site of infantile anxieties, of helplessness and disintegration. The audience is confronted by the first horrors of the Alien’s task, to seduce and lure solitary men to their death. To literally suck out all the interior space.

In my reading of the film, I consider some of the internal psychic mechanisms, which bring this primitive horror to life, broadly using a psychoanalytic framework to do so. I do not give a blow by blow account of the film, but prefer to concentrate on some key themes and moments of narrative shift, which, in my view, offer some insight that could be interesting for child psychotherapists to think about.

There are some potential paralells between the depiction of the male victims in the film and our child and adolescent patients, and how their experience of gender and sexuality can be thwarted and maladapted. Our child and adolescent patients can feel both seduced by and at the same time horrified when entering the consulting room, and all that the clinical setting may entail for them.There is also something significant in the film that we can think about, regarding how female clinicians’ bodies are ‘used’ and projected into by our child and adolescent patients, and how we as a profession can sometimes avoid thinking about our own sexuality in the consulting room, retreating into the safety and familiarity of the maternal.

Transforming Despair to Hope, by Monica Lanyado, Abingdon, Routledge, 2018, 174 pp., £24.99 (paperback), ISBN 978-1-138-064720

Kate Purdy

Kate Purdy

kateforsyth@blueyonder.co.uk

Kate Purdy  

In the introduction to her book, Monica Lanyado sets out her thesis – that some children come into the world with ‘nearly all the cards stacked against him or her from the start of life’ (p. xvii). However, she is quick also to point out that ‘it is important to remember […] that there have been, and often remain, many people involved in these troubled lives, who are trying to help, and keep on trying to help’ (p. xvii). In this way, the reader is introduced from the start to this book’s central preoccupation, which is clear from the title: how the despair experienced by these children and those around them might just possibly be transformed into hope.

In the first chapter, Lanyado explores some of the consequences of neglect and trauma. She refers to great nineteenth century literature, in which children lived in poverty, unable to rely on the adults around them to take care of them, experiencing trauma which embedded itself into their psyche. She cites Charles Dickens’ Oliver Twist and Victor Hugo’s Gavroche in Les Miserables, as characters which move the reader: ‘great literature enables the reader to identify with characters such as Oliver and Gavroche, and briefly get a sense of what it would be like to live their lives.’ (p. 2) She continues: ‘the children that this book is about are the survivors of similar starts to Oliver and Gavroche’. My feeling is that this is a book also about those ‘readers’ who are moved to try to help, and who hold out the possibility of hope in the face of what can feel like insurmountable despair.

Lanyado makes a harrowing list of the difficulties these children can carry with them, when removed from their birth families, explaining why it is so hard to care for them:

‘Their basic trust in any adult’s capacity to care for them has been fundamentally compromised by their birth parents’ inability to care for them. This lack of trust is transferred into any potential new relationship including the psychotherapeutic relationship, and results in the child using strong emotional defences to protect him or herself from further distress and trauma. These defences often become self-defeating, leading to further difficulties.’ (p. 3)

[[RunningHead]]

Editorial

Alexandra de Rementeria

Alexandra de Rementeria

Alexandra de Rementeria   alexandra.derementeria@childpsychotherapy.org.uk

I had the good fortune to be taking up my role at a point when this issue had already been conceived and was taking shape. My predecessor, Lydia Hartland-Rowe and our Editor, Maria Papadima, had invited short papers about the impact of the pandemic on the work of child psychotherapists in the UK and around the world. Like a short report from the frontline, these papers have immediacy. As a collection, they serve as a snapshot of what has been possible during this time, but I have also been surprised and impressed by how much reflection and processing is already entrained. It will, of course, be a very long time before we understand the scale or detail of how the pandemic has affected our world. We might expect that it will be longer still before we can really understand how we responded in the consulting room and why. However, these papers give us a sense of where we are now and how fruitful such explorations are going to continue to be.

This issue begins with a review of the literature available, pre-pandemic, on technology mediated therapy, by Maria Pozzi Monzo and Sara Micotti. Most of the subsequent short papers in this issue describe individual work with children and young people and these are loosely organised under the headings: The experience of the therapist, and: The setting, technology and the body. There are a further three papers describing infant observation, group work and supervision during the pandemic. Each set of papers begins with a commentary, drawing out the themes of each paper, so I will not address that here. Instead, in this editorial, I want to describe what excites me about these papers as a collection.

All authors seem to share a central theme regarding the way that remote work brought the loss of, and consequent need to reimagine, the psychoanalytic frame. Some might argue that making this choice – to work remotely – was a manic defence; that we failed to mourn what we could not save. If there are clinicians who chose not to offer any work remotely, we did not hear from them at this stage. Perhaps those papers have yet to come?

[[RunningHead]]

Commentary: The therapist

Maria Papadima

Maria Papadima

Maria Papadima  

It has been a challenging year to be working as psychotherapists. Our personal lives – our hopes, fears, yearnings, anxieties, strengths and weak spots – have inevitably bled into our work this year. We, together with our patients, have had to face an entirely new situation, posing key questions: how do we manage our daily lives, look after our families, yet at the same time be there for our patients? How do we absorb minor and major traumas, which sometimes have come at a dizzying pace, without losing our composure too much?

Sebastian Kohon’s words echoed with me: ‘what would it be like if a sighted group of visitors were forced to navigate this event [in the dark] with a clueless guide who had no experience of managing without sight?’ This year, we have indeed felt at times like clueless guides, frantically trying to process and digest what has often felt impossible to fully take in, at a pace that would allow us to both look after ourselves and attend to our patients.

The selection of papers that follows offers a glimpse into the minds and lives of child psychotherapists during this first year of Covid. What has it been like to face so many rapid changes, so much loss, so many adjustments to the setting? We have hardly had time to stand still and take stock this year, and these papers offer an opportunity to do so.

In my case, as a psychotherapist working with adolescents whom I sometimes had to see in person during the lockdowns, I recall my initial feelings of agitation when some of them refused to wear masks. The complex and guilt-inducing question of seeing some young people face-to-face, while others are not seen, entails frustrating and unsatisfying choices. Nikolas Antoniades’ paper, coming from Cyprus, illustrates the dilemmas involved in such decisions. I related to his thoughts: ‘I started feeling guilty about making these choices … as if I was breaking some ethical law, or indeed breaking the Law’.

Working some of the time in person, for me, involved both fear as well as relief and camaraderie when seeing colleagues in person. Working within a team, this year, has taken on a particular significance. Catherine Webster, writing from Scotland, talks of the ‘tight anxious feeling that had taken up residence’ in her and her colleagues, and the ‘strange tearfulness which was not specific to one thing but generalised and weaving in and out of the day’. She eloquently describes, at the same time, the closeness to her colleagues that she experienced and that kept her going.

Commentary: The setting, technology and the body

Elizabeth Francis

Elizabeth Francis

elizabeth.francis@oxfordhealth.nhs.uk

Elizabeth Francis  

It can be easy to forget how shocking it was in March 2020 not to be able to see our patients. The task at first seemed to be a salvaging operation, finding a way to keep in contact and sustain some containment for our patients, our colleagues and ourselves. Gradually, we became more used to new ways of working, doing therapy online or by telephone, meeting patients outside, or working in person while wearing PPE.

What kind of therapeutic work can be done remotely? How different has it been from working in the therapy room? What have been the costs and have there been benefits? What has surprised us?

Ehud Wolpe, a child and adolescent psychoanalyst in Israel, describes how the key tasks he undertook developed over the course of the pandemic, from efforts to preserve the therapist’s presence in the child’s psyche, towards maintaining continuity and therapeutic presence and holding a new, unfamiliar type of transference with new mediators – the screen or the mask. Wolpe found that he could maintain a holding therapeutic environment, but at the expense of more in-depth analytic work. Gillian Sloan Donachy, in the UK, was reminded of what had been lost in remote working when she was able to take some walks with a patient in their final sessions.

Michael Garcia and Amanda Hutchison, in the United States, both managed to establish some continuity between working in person and online. Hutchison leaned into the technical glitches that bedevil our online sessions, paying attention to their emotional meaning and using them as a window on the transference and countertransference. Garcia is highly aware of what is lost in an online session, but emphasises that the therapist’s ability to think through experience can be sustained through remote working and that this is what is essential in what we do.

Online therapy is not a disembodied process. We are present in our own spaces, as are our patients in theirs. Carolyn Hart, a British child psychotherapist, found that working online can give patients the chance to use their whole environment to communicate, letting the therapist know about their embodied experience, in ways that might not be so accessible in the therapy room. She points out the reality of the therapist receiving communications from patients through our body senses, even when not in the same room. Nupur Dhingra, in India, explores the impact on the therapist and on some patients of being the only body in the room. The gaze of the video screen involves patients seeing themselves, a gaze that one patient experienced as an outsider, critical point of view. My own patients have sometimes used this third presence as the object of a narcissistic gaze that can position me as someone being excluded, an admirer or voyeur. Dhingra eventually found that being the only body in the room could also be freeing, since she did not feel so pulled into the maternal transference.

Commentary: Groups

Alexandra de Rementeria

Alexandra de Rementeria

alexandra.derementeria@childpsychotherapy.org.uk

Alexandra de Rementeria  

These three final papers describe the work of groups of different kinds – an infant observation seminar group in Greece; a group for parents of children with disabilities in Italy; and a peer support group for child psychotherapists in Canada. Each group has a different function, but during the pandemic they all became extremely important for their participants as a container for all that the pandemic stirred.

The parents attending the clinical group in Italy found themselves, during Covid-19, at home, without support, caring full-time for children with complex care needs. The Greek observation seminar suffered an abrupt halt to their meetings with families, but soon the members realised that by meeting remotely as a seminar group they could think together of alternative ways to keep the connection with the infants and families. The Canadian peer supervision group, evocatively named the ‘Town Hall Group’, consists of a number of child therapists, working across different settings, who had a central point where they could meet and share their experiences. The Town Hall Group’s shared history and geography felt important, as the group now had to come together remotely and set to work on building a collective understanding of how to navigate remote therapy. Robin Holloway and his colleagues present a collection of clinical material discussed in this group during the pandemic.

Supervision, and writing about our work, have always served to develop and refine theory and technique; but under the pressures of the pandemic, the Town Hall Group became particularly energised and creative in their coming together. They note themselves that:

Although psychotherapy may be considered an individual/solitary activity, a two-person endeavour at its best, its development has always been a collective enterprise and the Town Hall has facilitated a potential space where creativity and hope can re-emerge.

This put me in mind of the armies of researchers who were able to develop vaccines so quickly, by abandoning the method of trying each new combination one after the other. Instead, they tried and compared a great number of possible ways forward all at once. In this context, we have all needed to get to know something entirely new as quickly as possible, and our Canadian colleagues show us that pooling our resources and experiences has been vital to this task.

Hamnet

by Maggie O’ Farrell, London, Tinder Press, 2020, 372 pp., £20 (hardback), ISBN 978-1472223791

Kate Purdy

Kate Purdy

Newcastle upon Tyne

Kate Purdy   kateforsyth@blueyonder.co.uk

Like many others in our line of work, back in March 2020 I found that along with reeling with the shock of living through a global pandemic, with all the worries, frustrations and powerless feelings which came along with this, I was also busier than ever working as a child psychotherapist in the local fostering team for children’s services. Conversations between friends and all over the media about what everyone would do with all this extra time as the country shut down seemed perplexing to me, as our team was struggling to adapt overnight to keep everything going. We were overwhelmed and working longer hours, while feeling fragmented and separated from colleagues and friends.

One way that I managed, once the working day was over, was the way I always manage when things are tough – or in fact when things are any way at all. I read. Literature was my first great and absolute love, long before the world of psychoanalysis made itself known to me. From my earliest childhood through to the present, books have always been my comfort and my absolute ‘thing’. As a child, I would read through family picnics and on long car journeys, and for hours at weekends. And now I still read every night before I sleep, even if it is only a few paragraphs at midnight of whichever novel I currently have ‘on the go’. I studied English Literature as an undergraduate and then American Literature as a post-graduate, and had a long and (mostly) happy career as an English teacher before I decided to re-train in child psychotherapy. I still miss the uncomplicated, optimistic pleasure in teaching Othello to sixth formers. There is something in beautiful words which offers a balm to the troubled soul.

So, I was very excited this year to read Hamnet. Maggie O’Farrell has long been one of my favourite authors, and linked with Shakespeare, how could this novel fail to delight and entertain? Hamnet is Shakespeare’s young son who dies, as he did in reality, in 1596 aged eleven of the plague, which he catches from his twin sister. What is amazing to me now is that as I started reading this in deepest lockdown, I did not have any sense that the plague was central to Hamnet. In addition, to my shame, I only had the faintest memory that Shakespeare had had a son named Hamnet, despite Hamlet being one of my favourite of Shakespeare’s plays. I later listened to Maggie O’Farrell speaking at the Hay Literary Festival about writing the book; she explained that in Shakespeare’s time, the names Hamlet and Hamnet were interchangeable.

Pale rider: the Spanish Flu of 1918 and how it changed the world

by Laura Spinney, London, Vintage, 2017, 332 pp., £10.99 (paperback), ISBN 978-1-78470-240-3 (pbk)

Maria Papadima

Maria Papadima

Enfield

Maria Papadima   maria.papadima@childpsychotherapy.org.uk

‘Against other things it is possible to obtain security,’

wrote the Greek philosopher Epicurus in the third century BC,

‘but when it comes to death we human beings all live in an unwalled city’

(pp. 19–20).

425 Before 2020, I don’t recall ever giving a second thought to the danger infectious diseases pose, either to myself personally, or more widely to the community within which I live. Partly this could be attributed to my wilful ignorance. But it is also true that there is only a limited number of things we can each hold in mind and worry about on a daily basis. Infections were not included on my own list of worries.

So, when the Covid-19 pandemic hit, I was taken by surprise. After the initial, abrupt reorganisation of my work and personal life, which we each had to deal with at the start of spring 2020, I turned to reading, to gain perspective and find my bearings in the situation. I swiftly found out what I should have already known: pandemics have (of course) occurred regularly throughout history. More interestingly, many of the superstitions, passionate debates, conspiracy theories and dilemmas we suddenly found ourselves surrounded by have a long history, threading through all previous pandemics too.

‘Pale Rider’ was published in 2017; it is Laura Spinney’s effort to map out the story of the Spanish Flu of 1918, a flu, it is worth saying, that didn’t originate anywhere near Spain. The Spanish Flu was ‘the most deadly pandemic in human history. It is estimated that five hundred million people contracted it – a third of the global population in 1918 – and that between fifty and a hundred million of them died’ (Francis, 2018). That pandemic, I learnt from ‘Pale Rider’, had significant differences from the current one, not just in terms of the numbers of people affected, but also, crucially, in the fact that children were much more vulnerable to it. Yet surprisingly, Spinney notes: ‘When asked what was the biggest disaster of the twentieth century, almost nobody answers the Spanish flu’ (p. 4). She points out that -

The Spanish flu is remembered personally, not collectively. Not as a historical disaster, but as millions of discrete, private tragedies. (p. 4)

Covid-19 pandemic, digital technology and cyberspace, disinhibition effect, digital natives and digital immigrants, cross-modal attunement

This paper focuses on the use of technology in psychoanalytic psychotherapy with children and adults. The necessity to use Zoom, WhatsApp and the telephone was suddenly brought about for all of us with the outbreak of the Coronavirus pandemic in March 2020. In-person treatments, including those which were established and those which had just begun, had to be switched on to new means of communication. This paper looks at a number of writings, considering them in chronological order, to show the progression and evolution of thinking on this crucial topic.

Countertransference, paternal function, maternal function, pandemic, setting, differentiation, Covid-19

Some challenges to clinicians’ use of their countertransference responses during the pandemic are explored, in relation to direct clinical work and supervision. Changes to the setting, shared existential anxieties, as well as a sense that authority figures may be compromised, affect the structure of the clinical encounter. It can be harder in this context to differentiate the anxieties and defences of patient, clinician and supervisor, making it more difficult to be guided reliably by countertransference feelings.

The paper reflects on the authors’ observations regarding the handling of the Covid-19 pandemic within the context of child and adolescent psychoanalytic psychotherapy in Greece. The specific conditions in Greece during the first general lockdown are described, and the necessary modifications to the therapeutic framework with latency children and adolescents are discussed. The authors share their thoughts about the ways they tried to keep the connection with their patients alive, in the face of the first wave of the coronavirus crisis.

Editorial

Lydia Hartland-Rowe

Lydia Hartland-Rowe

lydia.hartlandrowe@childpsychotherapy.org.uk

Lydia Hartland-Rowe  

This editorial is written at a time unlike any other, towards the end of the first wave of the Covid-19 global pandemic, and in the middle of a worldwide response to structural racism sparked by the death of George Floyd in the United States. There is no doubt that over the next months and years, we will see our literature expand in relation to what these events mean, and what their implications might be for psychoanalytic clinical theory and practice with children and young people, parents and families.

Apart from the research digest that helpfully draws together abstracts relating to telephone and video therapy, the papers and articles in this journal emerged from a time before the current struggles and preoccupations. In their breadth and range of interest, however, they highlight how our community of practice has been able to respond with flexibility and interest to the challenges of what we are all facing globally as human beings and as psychoanalytic practitioners. What comes across from the work in this edition is the curiosity, readiness to explore, and depth of engagement that are alive in the minds of those who work psychoanalytically with children; these papers illustrate some of the different places towards which that instinct to understand more has been directed.

The first group of articles in the journal are full-length papers with a particular area of interest under examination. A foundation of our psychoanalytic work is our own experience of being a patient; the first paper by Coralie Lasvergnas-Garcia has this experience as a focus, asking important questions and exploring themes that may encourage further debate and discussion regarding analytic treatment during training.

Next, Deborah Marks looks at the centrality of work with parents as another foundation in the frame, allowing and supporting the work undertaken with children. Crasnow et al. provide an account from the practitioners’ perspectives of work with parents in a homeless hostel, part of a strong tradition across the child psychotherapy profession and pre-clinical workforce in making use of a psychoanalytic framework to inform working relationships. Jenkins et al. also present a way of working in a setting outside the clinical environment, with an account that adds to the growing literature on clinical practice in educational settings, with communities who might otherwise be excluded from access to treatment.

Editorial

Lydia Hartland-Rowe

Lydia Hartland-Rowe

lydia.hartlandrowe@childpsychotherapy.org.uk

Lydia Hartland-Rowe  

I write this editorial for the second edition of 2020 at the end of an extraordinary and unsettling period of global uncertainty, and on the brink of another, as the next wave of the Covid-19 pandemic starts to gather force in many parts of the world. There is no doubt that the year so far has been a complex and turbulent one, with the impact of the Coronavirus on our physical, mental and economic health, as well as with the important issues that activity related to the Black Lives Matter movement has re-exposed. Our next edition will feature a collection of shorter pieces from the international community, giving accounts of what has been experienced and learned from the global phenomena that have been so preoccupying for all of us.

The current edition features articles and papers that pre-date the past months, giving us an important link to our ongoing interests and areas for development, but still offering scope for new ways of working clinically, thinking theoretically, and interacting creatively with the structures and frameworks in which our work takes place, as well as with colleagues from connected disciplines.

Papers from Andrew Dawson and Adam Goren highlight the dual focus that needs to be held by psychoanalytic child psychotherapists in relation to our core aim of working with the vulnerabilities and scope for development of the children encountered in our work. Dawson brings the reality of the contemporary commissioning frameworks in which much clinical work takes place, examining it in close and meaningful connection with work with children in the care system. He gives an account of collaborative work that included the development and use of a clinical formulation tool. This powerful account of the possibility for embedding psychoanalytic child psychotherapy practice and thinking into a model that also satisfies wider system needs is a hugely helpful model for how we can join up internal and external world pressures, in a way that meets the needs of children. Goren’s paper focuses more closely on work with traumatised adopted children and their parents, building on a growing number of Journal publications on the theme, by authors such as Simon Cregeen (Volume 43, 2017), and further highlighting the need to be alert to the complex dynamics in the internal and external world of children who have been traumatised – almost certainly something we will need to understand more about, as current events unfold.

Psychoanalysis, Neuroscience and the Stories of Our Lives. The Relational Roots of Mental Health, by Sarah Sutton, London, Routledge, 2020, 127 pp., £24.99 (paperback), ISBN: 13 9781138364301

Robert Fleming

Robert Fleming

rwkfleming@me.com

Robert Fleming  

Sarah Sutton has trawled deeply through three decades of brain research, to digest the key lessons from the numerous discoveries of neuroscience. She presented some of them in her previous book, ‘Being taken in: The framing relationship’ (Sutton, 2014). This most recent book is, I would argue, an even more valuable treasure trove of interdisciplinary findings for Child and Adolescent Psychotherapy. With huge skill, Sutton presents complex ideas with clarity and humour. Throughout the book, she shows us that psychoanalysis was often correct about the functioning of the mind. However, Sutton is not afraid to challenge some of the positions that are not supported by the research evidence. The book is relatively short (127 pages), but it is crammed with significance. I suspect that it will become an essential must-read book for many clinicians.

The main theme of the book is that we are all essentially interdependent. The relational roots of the mind start from our very first moments, and can only be properly understood in the context of our family (and intergenerational history), and the wider social context. Mental health symptoms do not arise from an individual’s own fallibilities.

Sutton begins by examining the very act of perception, arguing that we give all experiences meaning, based on the existing store of matches. For survival and adaptive reasons, everything we take in is mediated by our early relationships from the very start of life. Every decision we make is based on filtered perceptual information that is largely unconscious. What we notice and how we respond is thus experience-dependent. It would seem that neuronal connections that fit with the mediating frame (of relationships) are reinforced, and those that are not are pruned. (This is the neurobiology of transference.) In this way, Sutton can link ‘seeing, being and identity’. She writes,

‘Essentially, observation is formative: both what we see and how we are seen – consequently, how we see ourselves in that social relational context – forms the basis for identity, in work and social settings every bit as much as in family groups.’ (p. 22)

Katherine Shillito

Katherine Shillito

Katherine Shillito   Katherine Shillito is a child and adolescent psychodynamic counsellor at the Brent Centre for Young People, London, UK, where she works in in-house, schools, private and Youth Offending services.CONTACT Katherine Shillito Katherine.shillito@brentcentre.org.uk Brent Centre for Young People, London, UK
Covid-19, adolescents, psychotherapy, teletherapy

The paper offers a personal reflection on working for a charity offering psychotherapeutic help to adolescents in an inner London borough during the Covid-19 pandemic. The paper highlights the importance of considering the adolescent’s material circumstances together with their developmental needs when setting up remote work. It explores the unconscious meaning of remote contact and of the adolescent’s choice of a teletherapy modality, as well as the role of fantasy and the body in the absence of visual information. The paper also considers the impact remote working has had on the boundaries and dynamics of psychotherapy.

He worked clinically in CAMHS NHS teams and held a Senior Child Psychotherapist position, in a service supervisor role. He has been involved in Education and Training at the Tavistock and Portman NHS Foundation Trust as a visiting lecturer, and co-Organising Tutor for the Introductory course: Developing a diverse child and adolescent workforce (CPD64). Recently he has relocated in Nicosia, Cyprus, where he works in private practice. In collaboration with local prematurity organisations and other professionals, he has been active in putting in place European Standards of Neonatal Care for Mental Health as set by the European Foundation for the Care of Newborn Infants (EFCNI), by providing parental support in NICU, running reflective practice groups for NICU staff, and providing (parent) infant mental health training. He is a also a peer reviewer for the Journal of Child Psychotherapy.CONTACT Nikolas Antoniades Nikolas.Antoniades@outlook.com Flat 501, 12 Nearchou Cliridi, 1087, Nicosia, Cyprus
Face-to-face psychotherapy, psycho-social implications, Covid-19 lockdown; unconscious to unconscious communications, presence of the therapist

In this short paper, I want to examine the function, and a number of ethical and clinical dilemmas, in deciding to continue to work in the consulting room with an 18-year-old boy during the first Covid-19 lockdown in Cyprus. This patient displayed a borderline organisation of the schizoid type, with a marked false self presentation. To understand this work, I build on Winnicott’s theories, as well as Monica Lanyado’s ideas. Lanyado explores how the presence of the therapist and that of the therapy itself acquire functions beyond those commonly defined within the psychoanalytic framework – in this case, due to the nature of the collectively experienced phenomenon of the lockdown. Local circumstances, restrictions and realities in Cyprus are described, as they occurred at the time of the first Covid-19 lockdown, showing how the patient’s pathology became intertwined with the above conflicts and dilemmas that I faced as his psychotherapist, and as a fellow member of the local and global society. I argue that under such unusual conditions, psychotherapist and patient become part of the same local and global collective, and only if they work ‘hand in hand’ can they survive a collectively experienced trauma, at a time when most human contact was forbidden by law.

Catherine Webster

Catherine Webster

Kirkcaldy
Fife, UK

Catherine Webster   Catherine Webster is a Psychoanalytic Child and Adolescent Psychotherapist. She completed her training with the Scottish Institute of Human Relations in 2013. Prior to her psychotherapy training she first worked as a drama and movement therapist and play specialist in London and later trained to be a play therapist. She moved to Edinburgh and worked as a freelance play therapist in primary schools and as a trainer for Children in Scotland. She has worked with children and adolescents for over 30 years and has also worked in family centres in Los Angeles, USA and Canberra, Australia. She now works for NHS Fife at Sea View, a CAMHS specialist sexual trauma project and also for the Infant Mental Health Team.CONTACT Catherine Webster catherine.webster@nhs.scot Seaview Project, Sexual Trauma Service/CAMHS, Whyteman’s Brae Hospital, Whyteman’s Brae, Kirkcaldy, Fife KY1 2ND, UK

In this paper I explore the stages of shock, adjustment and grief involved in trying to offer psychotherapy to children and adolescents in the first wave of the UK Covid 19 pandemic. I discuss the loss of the live experience alongside the absence of my colleagues due to the transition to remote working. I touch on Freud’s paper ‘Mourning and melancholia’ and consider how losing the physical presence of patients and colleagues in time led to what the American psychologist Freudenberger termed‘ burn-out.’ I discuss Freudenberger’s concept and propose that although we did show signs and symptoms of burn-out it never became a chronic condition but was episodic in nature. I suggest that we have been living through a time when we have been confronted by personal and collective anxieties about death and dying. I touch on the idea of ‘resilience’ and my observation that it is founded on interdependence. I also suggest that we can be helped by our training, analysis and supervision and need to use these in conscious ways in order to look out for ourselves at a time when there are very real external fears and anxieties.

Maria Pini   Maria Grazia Pini is a child and adolescent psychotherapist. Member of AMHPPIA, Associazione Martha Harris Psicoterapia Psicoanalitica dell’Infanzia e dell’Adolescenza, Florence, Italy. Teacher and Organising Director at the Centro Studi Martha Harris Clinical Training, Florence, Italy.
Parents, working online, pandemic, lockdown

The authors reflect on the experience of working with groups of parents of children with mental or physical disabilities, which had started long before the Covid lockdown and continued online after a brief interruption due to the pandemic. The reflection is still ongoing, and it is not possible for the moment to draw definitive conclusions. The experience of the groups working online, despite the initial mistrust, has proved useful, albeit in a peculiar way, different from before. In a group already formed and accustomed to sharing anxieties and problems, it was possible to maintain the vitality of relationships, the group continuing to function as a thinking container. The participants had the opportunity to reflect on the new experiences they were having at home with their children, even discovering in themselves new parenting skills. The inevitable changes in the setting have required for the psychotherapists leading the groups to pay special attention in maintaining their psychoanalytic listening skills, and they have also triggered some questions, which still need to be thought about.

Carolyn Hart

Carolyn Hart

Carolyn Hart   Carolyn Hart is a child and adolescent psychotherapist who trained at the Tavistock Clinic, London. She has spent much of her career to date working with ‘looked after’ children. This experience kindled her interest in the biology of trauma and embodied cognition. In 2017 she completed a diploma in online therapy and has for several years been using remote ways of working in her independent practice.CONTACT Carolyn Hart cjv4g@mac.com www.hartfelttherapy.co.uk
Transference relationship, embodied process, video mediated, metaphor, evoked feelings

This article is concerned with embodied process and the need to attend to evoked emotion in order to support the transference relationship. I look briefly at Lakoff and Johnson’s work on linguistic metaphor and the way, through embodied cognition, it shapes our conceptual world. Through the use of clinical vignettes, I illustrate how some of my clients use a combination of technology and embodied process to evoke strong emotional and physiological countertransference responses in me. One of the advantages of working online is that, given the chance, our clients use their whole environment to communicate. They access software and use hardware, including furniture, to let us know about their embodied experience. Some of what they use might not be so accessible during face-to-face sessions. I have found that paying attention to what they bring and the emotions aroused enhances our communication and the transference relationship.

The experience of working via tele video in Australia during the Covid-19 pandemic

Ruth Neven

Ruth Neven

Camberwell
Australia

Ruth Neven   Ruth Schmidt Neven PhD is a child psychotherapist and clinical psychologist. She is the founder director of the Centre for Child and Family Development in Melbourne Australia and was previously inaugural Chief Child Psychotherapist at the Royal Children’s Hospital in Melbourne. In addition to her extensive clinical work, she has run training programmes throughout Australia and internationally, based on her model that conceptualizes links between the core developmental task, and interactive child parent assessment and therapy. She is the author of four books, the most recent being Time-limited Psychodynamic Psychotherapy with Children and Adolescents: An interactive approach (Routledge, 2017). She has published articles and chapters on clinical work that include attention deficit disorder, under-fives counselling and critiques of contemporary pathology-based child and family mental health practices. She was a keynote speaker at the first Key Debate on Child Psychotherapy Research held in October 2018 in London.CONTACT Ruth Schmidt Neven ccfdau@ozemail.com.au Centre for Child and Family Development, P. O. Box 14600, Camberwell, Victoria 3124, Australia
Melbourne Australia, the clinical stance, boundaries and space, transference issues, assessment and diagnosis of adolescents, prodromal signs and symptoms

This paper examines some of the challenges involved in working via tele video in Melbourne Australia during the Covid-19 pandemic. Several factors are identified that contribute to the success of tele video with patients. These include the maintenance of a clinical stance that enables a direct managing of the issues of boundaries and space in the tele video setting. Despite the author’s earlier reservations, the tele video experience has identified how powerfully transference issues are communicated and how these appear to transcend what we may have assumed to be the limitations of the tele video setting. Attention is paid to what is seen, revealed, and recognised during the tele video sessions and how these elements contribute to creating a three-dimensional experience within a two-dimensional space. The question of carrying out assessment and diagnosis online is discussed in the context of work with adolescents to clearly delineate between ordinary transient reactions and pathological or prodromal reactions in the adolescent.

Leeds

Deborah Marks   deborahsusanmarks@gmail.com

At the age of twelve, Lemn Sissay lost the only family he had ever known. He was handed back to his long-term foster parents who had cared for him since babyhood. The consequences were devastating. His memoir offers a forensic investigation into belonging, betrayal and catastrophic loss.

Lemn’s life began in a unit for unmarried mothers and babies. His mother had come to the UK from Ethiopia in order to study. Pregnant and alone in a foreign country, Lemn’s mother was not in a position to care for him, so, at two months old, he went into care. His mother was pressured to sign adoption papers and give her baby up. She refused to sign, hoping to have her son back when she could manage. She returned home but did try later on to reclaim her son. However, the British authorities made this impossible.

Lemn was renamed Norman and put up for long-term fostering, with the assurance to his new parents that they would be his ‘forever’ parents. ‘Norman’s’ foster parents were white Christians who were strict. He grew up to be a curious, charming, lively and intelligent child, who was eager to please. His foster parents went on to have three further birth children. The book hints at tensions and rivalries following the arrival of his brother. As Sissay approached puberty, his parents felt ‘the devil had got into him’. He began stealing biscuits and when confronted, denied his ‘crimes’. Ordinary misdemeanours and complicated unconscious communications were misunderstood and pathologised. Gradually, an atmosphere of suspicion and blame led to a spiral, in which Lemn was tested, judged and found by his foster parents, in the cruellest of reversals, to be guilty of ‘not loving them’.

What is extraordinary about this memoir is the form it takes. We are invited to read reports written by the social worker and other professionals. These were never meant to be seen outside the confines of a professional audience. Sissay is made the object of a disciplinary gaze and the reader becomes the voyeur of this objectifying process. Online child psychotherapy and the pandemic – vignettes from the Canadian Association of Psychoanalytic Child Therapists

Robin Holloway , Felipe Hinrichsen , Fӓggie Oliver and Robyn Weddepohl

Robyn Weddepohl

Toronto
Canada

Robyn Weddepohl   Robyn Weddepohl is a Registered Psychotherapist. She is a graduate of CICAPP (The Canadian Institute for Child and Adolescent Psychoanalytic Psychotherapy). Robyn is now in private practice in Ontario with an interest in group and individual therapy with ASD individuals.
Containment, digital screens, online psychotherapy, osmotic anxieties, therapeutic frame, Town Hall meetings

At a time when psychoanalytic psychotherapists are struggling worldwide to provide ongoing psychotherapy to children and adolescents during the current pandemic, this paper provides three vignettes, which focus on the impact of the pandemic and of providing psychotherapy online. These vignettes elaborate on contributions made to ‘Town Hall’ meetings of the Canadian Association of Psychoanalytic Child Therapists. We describe some of what we have learned in our efforts to provide online therapy during this disjointed time. We conclude by reflecting on the crucial importance of peer groups meeting together to contain our own pandemic anxieties, to maintain the therapeutic frame in online treatment, and to be supportive of the internal psychic frames of our patients, all of which have been battered during the pandemic.

Child protection, formulation, personality development, well-being, functional, CAMHS, complex trauma, learning disability

This paper outlines the development of a formulation tool for use in child psychotherapy practice. This was developed in response to Child Protection legislation and practice, which was shown to be different across the four nations of the United Kingdom, and details a National Practice Model that is part of Scottish Government Legislation. The paper discusses the way that child psychotherapy can make a unique contribution in the treatment of a child, showing positive progressions in child well-being and in the functional aspects of a child’s personality development. The paper uses a detailed case example to demonstrate the use of the formulation tool under discussion. The author suggests that a structured approach allows the child psychotherapist to make best use of their whole training and observational skills, as required by each case.

Research digest: the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic on child, adolescent, young adult, and family mental health

Rachel Acheson

Rachel Acheson

Enfield
United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

Rachel Acheson   CONTACT Rachel Acheson Rachel.acheson117@gmail.com Barnet Enfield and Haringey CAMHS, Enfield SAFE, Baytree House, Christchurch Close, Enfield, United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland

This issue’s research digest focuses on the emerging literature concerning the impact of the Covid-19 pandemic on the mental health of children, adolescents, young adults, and families. This is currently an area of great concern internationally, with those working in the field attempting to understand to what extent, and in what ways, the measures governments have put in place to curb the spread of coronavirus have affected mental health.

The sudden onset of the pandemic, and the fact that it has led to individuals having to isolate from one another, has ramifications for the type of research that has so far been possible. While some of the research published in this issue’s research digest may not be of the same quality as that of previous issues, it is impressive to consider how much has been achieved in such a short space of time and in such restricted conditions. Also pertinent is that different countries have experienced and managed the pandemic differently, and so there may be limits to how much we can learn from each other’s research at this point. At the time of writing, there is only one published study from the UK (Bignardi et al., 2021).

While the majority of studies summarised below have shown an increase in emotional and mental health difficulties during the pandemic, it is also interesting to note that this is not a universal finding, with two studies finding no change in the indices measured (Xiang et al., 2020; Isumi et al., 2020). Some studies included look at the effect of the pandemic in non-clinical populations of young people (for example, Zhou et al., 2020), while others examine how it may affect or exacerbate pre-existing conditions (Tanir et al., 2020). Some of the research included concerning the mental health impact on young adults has used interesting methodologies, such as examining the effect of housing conditions on emotional wellbeing (Amerio et al., 2020), or comparing students’ social networks before and during the pandemic (Elmer et al., 2020). Unsurprisingly, much research has focussed on the effect of the pandemic on parents, and this review contains a wealth of material exploring and highlighting this.

Personal analysis is a central requirement for the training of UK child and adolescent psychotherapists and is part-funded by the National Health Service in the UK. Empirical research on the significance of analysis for the professional development of child psychotherapists is virtually non-existent. Some empirical literature supports the importance of personal psychotherapy for the training of adult psychotherapists, but the differences between adult and child psychotherapy make the findings of this literature tenuous and difficult to apply directly to the child psychotherapy training. This study aims to explore this issue by studying qualified child psychotherapists’ views on the role that personal analysis has played in their professional development, with a particular focus on the ways in which it affects the relationships they form with their patients. Semi-structured interviews were conducted with six UK-based child and adolescent psychotherapists, focusing on their views about the role of personal analysis in their professional development during training and post-qualification. These interviews were audio-recorded and analysed using thematic analysis. Thematic analysis of the interview material points to three main themes: the holistic experience of being a patient; the supportive aspect of analysis during training; and factors associated with the impact of the analysis being part of the training. In brief, it appears that personal analysis during training enabled the participants to learn things they would not have been able to learn in any other way; however, the close links between the training schools and the analysts were seen as a more controversial topic.

Research digest: psychological interventions via telephone and Internet

This edition’s digest pulls together research into the remote delivery of psychotherapy, online or by phone. It includes an outcome study of Internet-based psychodynamic psychotherapy for adolescents experiencing depression (Lindqvist et al., 2020); a qualitative exploration of the experiences of Singaporean primary school children accessing counselling via a live chat portal (Kit, Teo, Tan & Park, 2019); and a feasibility study of a group videoconferencing intervention for parents of children with a life-threatening illness (Rayner et al., 2016). It also includes studies examining clinicians’ experiences of using remote technology to deliver therapy (Cipolletta & Mocellin, 2018), including those who are psychoanalytically orientated (Trub & Magaldi, 2017). Two further articles are concerned with developing, or training clinicians to offer, remote therapeutic interventions for people living in rural areas, with little access to therapeutic services (Duncan, Velasquez & Nelson, 2014; McCord, Saenz, Armstrong & Elliott, 2015).

Since many therapists are having to change and adapt practices to deliver remote psychotherapy in the absence of formal training or research, we have also included a paper offering theoretical ideas and observations on offering psychoanalysis via videoconference (Gutiérrez, 2017). In addition, we include a review of the literature on ‘psychological telehealth’ (Perle & Nierenberg, 2013), a systematic review of studies comparing telephone and face-to-face therapy (Irvine et al., 2020), and a rapid review of the evidence on the psychological impact of quarantine (Brooks et al., 2020). All of these may be particularly informative for clinicians needing to react and adapt quickly to remote working with children and families under lockdown.

Finally, a helpful review of current evidence relating to the virtual and digital delivery of interventions for children and young people (Jack Martin et al., 2020) published by the Early Intervention Foundation, can be found at www.eif.org.uk.

Coronavirus, online, technology, transference, adolescents, psychoanalytic psychotherapy

This paper reflects on some of the author’s experiences conducting psychoanalytic psychotherapy remotely during the coronavirus pandemic. The author takes E M. Forster’s famous epigraph ‘Only connect’ as a starting point for reflecting on the nature of connecting in therapy when that work is mediated by technology. In particular, the author discusses his uncertainty about the impact of a digital format on the transference relationship. Three vignettes from the author’s clinical work with adolescents are presented to expand upon this theme, before the author concludes that a transference relationship can survive, and sometimes thrive, across a digital distance.

Parent work, parent psychotherapy, therapeutic alliance, psycho-education, preventative work, sole clinician

This paper argues that parent work should occupy a more central place in the work of child psychotherapists, as it fosters an increase in parents' skill, insight and growth in the service of their offspring. Parent work is also crucial in strengthening the alliance with the therapist who sees the child or young person. The capacity to offer parents psycho-education, respectful challenge, empathy and support at a deeper level than is currently possible is likely to be cost effective, even though it may require more clinical hours devoted to the carer/s. Clinical time can be saved by the opportunity to engage in preventative work, briefer work and potentially more secure and enduring outcomes with the child.

In this commentary, we want to expand on some of the key concepts presented in an interesting paper that was recently published in the Journal of Child Psychotherapy. While some of the published papers by child psychotherapists are presented, and thus discussed, at conferences, we don’t often get the opportunity to thoroughly discuss and ‘digest’ much of this thought-provoking clinical and research work. We thus read Grossfeld et al.’s recent paper with interest, as it raises a number of interesting clinical and research dilemmas. We hope that this commentary opens up a space for further dialogue, with the view to enrich each other’s work, at times by offering alternative perspectives.

This interesting, well-structured research paper by Grossfeld et al. (2019) begins to address a widely recognised question in our profession: how can we meaningfully conceptualise and assess the process and outcomes of psychoanalytic treatment? Unlike other treatment modalities (e.g. Cognitive Behavioural Therapy), the processes involved in psychoanalytic psychotherapy, including child psychotherapy, are often intangible and hard to describe precisely, even with the best of intentions. As child psychotherapists, many of us work in multidisciplinary teams, in the NHS and other clinical settings. It is thus of particular importance today, in that context of multidisciplinary working, and during a time characterised by an emphasis on evidence based treatments, that we are able to adequately account for our work and its outcomes.

These clinical and research debates should concern us, as child psychotherapists, and we should dedicate time and effort in our work to engage in them and to attempt to provide some answers. In some cases, our attempt to address the question of ‘research in child psychotherapy’ could simply involve opening up new questions, which is also a valid way to enter into this much needed dialogue. Our overarching epistemology as a profession, we believe, should be one that strives to generate a type of knowledge that is constantly evolving, while relying on solid methodological foundations. So the question is: how do we disrupt the quest for certainty that dominates our current health care systems, while making sure we are able to offer our own robust research findings? In this commentary, we ask the reader to keep this question at the forefront of their mind.

Transference, countertransference, projective identification, treatment setting, telehealth, Covid-19

The Covid-19 global pandemic has, for the moment, upended the traditional setting for analysing transference and countertransference dynamics, vital components to the work of psychoanalytic child psychotherapy. The physicality of the customary treatment setting provides a basis for the experiences of containment and understanding, along with the corresponding and familiar technical considerations within that setting. The absence of these fixed physical elements when transferring cases to virtual and other non-conventional settings points to a new set of technical challenges. How do we understand projective identification, transference and countertransference with children when the modified setting does not inherently afford a child the physical means to make contact with the consulting room as a container? What resources do we have as clinicians for persevering through the psychoanalytic process, in the face of the current global uncertainties? In this paper, I outline some of the theoretical underpinnings in psychoanalytic child psychotherapy that elucidate the challenges to the work I have encountered with my child patients during the pandemic, and explore the clinical implications stemming from those challenges.

This short paper is a brief exploration of working towards an ending, during the global pandemic, with a young woman who had previously been attending for once-weekly face-to-face psychotherapy. Silence, silent, adolescent, adolescence, psychoanalytic psychotherapy, STPP, PICS

Psychotherapy process research is important in developing technique and enhancing clinical skills. Silence, as an aspect of child and adolescent psychoanalytic psychotherapy, has been a neglected area of research, despite it being acknowledged as an often challenging yet therapeutically useful aspect of the work. This study aims to explore silence in adolescent psychoanalytic psychotherapy, by studying the emergence of silence in therapy sessions. Three Short-Term Psychoanalytic Psychotherapies of adolescents with depression were used in the study, and silences occurring in six sessions of each therapy were coded, using the Pausing Inventory Categorization System (PICS). Findings showed that, in the three therapies sampled, almost one-third of session time was spent on average in silence, and most of this silence was coded as ‘obstructive’. Moreover, the amount of silence in every stage of therapy was different for each patient-therapist dyad. Follow-up interviews conducted with the adolescents were analysed using thematic analysis, and showed that the adolescents generally expressed negative feelings about silence in their therapy. Analysis suggests that the majority of the silence in these therapies related to conflict, which could be viewed as both an aspect of the developmental stage of adolescence, and a symptom of depression. These findings suggest that silences may not always be therapeutically productive in adolescent therapy, even if they are considered to be so in psychotherapy with adults, and so adaptations in therapeutic technique are required.

Child psychotherapy, playroom, Covid-19, coronavirus, trauma, face masks

The coronavirus outbreak required, among many changes and restrictions, a sudden and abrupt transition to online psychotherapy. This transition presented especially huge challenges to child psychotherapists. But as weeks and months have passed, and the virus has stayed with us, as our state of crisis has become routine, we are facing new and even greater challenges. We are back to the clinic with our young patients, but we are doing our therapeutic work while facing the danger of infection, wearing face masks, and being required to keep physical distance from each other. At the same time, children and parents, as well as the therapist herself, suffer from the consequences of the prolonged situation of crisis: there is anxiety, depression, and what seems worst of all, a sinking into apathy and indifference. Building on the evocative paper by Betty Joseph Thinking about the playroom, I will offer some preliminary insights into this (almost) impossible situation, in the context of our effort to keep our work, our patients and ourselves, alive and well.

Autism, psychosis, sensory integration, autisto-psychotic spectrum, child psychoanalysis, transference

In this article, I describe the psychoanalysis of a girl on the Autisto-Psychotic Spectrum and her struggle to emerge out of a severe autistic pathological organisation. At the beginning of her analysis, the girl was in a state of autistic confusion, which was manifested as a sensorial lack of colour differentiation. Following interpretative working-through of her deep anxieties-of-being, she established a sensorial-emotional ‘wall’, leading to a consolidation of a previously precarious primary splitting. This, in turn, led to a better capacity for emotional perception and differentiation. Further interpretation of her paranoid-schizoid anxieties enabled a gradual emergence of relatedness, communication, concern, and some integration and reparation. Moreover, as the girl’s linking functions, psychic space, object relations and integration improved, her sensory, perceptual and motor skills and integrative capacities improved as well. She eventually emerged into the emotional and sensorial ‘land of colours’. Thus, psychoanalytic psychotherapy, with its linking and mantling functions, proved to be indispensable for both her development, as well as for structural changes in her sensory-perceptual experience.

Patsy Ryz

It is a privilege to have been asked to write this review of Mary Morgan’s long awaited book on the psychoanalysis of couples; a book that encompasses the history and development of clinical and theoretical concepts, as practised at Tavistock Relationships (TR).

It feels particularly apt to be reviewing this book for the Journal of Child Psychotherapy, not only because I have trained both in child psychotherapy and couple psychotherapy but also because of the strong links between these two areas of clinical practice.

… as a child psychotherapist I have often experienced situations in which the couple’s difficulties are very firmly lodged in the child who then becomes the identified patient. In such circumstances addressing the couple issues can be problematic because the parents have not signed up for couple work and the therapist may feel she doesn’t have permission or expertise to venture into that area. (Ryz, 2018, pp. 192/3)

When considering further training, this had been one of the main reasons I eventually chose to train to work with couples, rather than with individual adults.

As stated in the editor’s forward of Morgan’s book: ‘This is the first book to describe in detail a method of therapy that has been under development for 70 years, since the founding of the Family Discussion Bureau in 1948’. (Abse, 2019, p. ix)

The book is beautifully written, in a clear and simple style that belies the depth and complexity of the concepts outlined, offering the reader an A–Z-like guide to couple therapy. As well as referencing the ‘contemporary influences of other psychoanalytic approaches to couples, particularly from an international perspective’, (ibid) the book includes the author’s seminal ideas on ‘the couple state of mind’ (Morgan, 2001, 2005, 2019), a concept which forms the cornerstone of her work and of the clinical practice at TR, an aspect of which is explored earlier in this issue by Mary Morgan herself.

This concept is rooted in the idea that in order to understand a couple’s difficulties, we have to think of the couple relationship as the patient. This involves looking at what each person contributes to the relationship and at what they, as a couple, create together, both consciously and unconsciously. Morgan suggests that the therapist’s ‘capacity to take a third position’ in relation to the couple – that is, ‘being able to be subjectively involved with both individuals, but also at the same time, being able to stand outside the relationship and observe the couple’ (Morgan, 2001, p. 17) is crucial in establishing and maintaining a couple state of mind. By ‘keeping the relationship in mind’ and directing interpretations ‘at what the couple create together’ (Morgan, 2001, p. 18), the therapist becomes an objective third, adopting a kind of participant-observer position. The author also argues that the relationship itself can become established ‘as a psychic object’ in its own right, to ‘which the couple relates symbolically and can feel contained by’ (Colman, 1993; Ruszczynski, 1998; Morgan, 2005).

This paper is a discussion of the experience of conducting psychotherapy sessions over the phone during the Covid pandemic. It explores the constraints and advantages of psychotherapy over the phone. Couple relationships, parenting, internal creative couple, couple psychotherapy

In this paper, the idea of an internal creative couple is explored in relation to parenting. The internal creative couple is seen as an outcome of psychic development, which may or may not have occurred, been impaired or temporarily lost. Examples of the way this can affect the couple and their parenting are given, elaborated through clinical illustrations. The process of psychic development enabling this capacity is described, highlighting several stages that seem crucial, though it is important to note that this development does not necessarily occur in a linear way, and involves returning to, and reworking at different developmental points in life. Creative couple relating, both internally and as manifested in couple and parenting relationships, is challenging and not always possible. Several reasons why this might be so are given.

On Intersubjective Aspects of Autism. The ‘Lightduress’ of Human Contact

Yaakov Roitman PHD

Yaakov Roitman

Kalman Bialer 6, Rehovot, Israel
roitmany@gmail.com

Yaakov Roitman   Clinical psychologist and supervisor at the Center of Research and Treatment of Autism (the Association for Children at Risk) and at private practice.
ASD, intersubjective, Ogden, Bion, autistic-contiguous position, Winnicott

In this article, I propose that some autistic states can be seen as a defensive organisation utilised to cope with the threat of the ‘light’ of human contact. An autistic child-patient may perceive the therapist’s separateness as an overwhelming threat, expressed in the way a therapist plays with him. This may feel thus to the patient as a threatening ‘light’. In this work, I argue that the therapist must survive their feeling, involving the idea that the way they are playing with the child-patient is destructive. The therapist must come to recognise that the part of the patient through which he or she perceives separateness is not only a developmental achievement, but also, for the child-patient, a catastrophic change. The therapist’s ability to see the separateness of patient and therapist as a catastrophe helps them be attuned to the child’s fear of the light of human contact. I describe a therapy in which these considerations, alive in my mind as I played with a seven-year-old girl, helped her recover from an autistic-psychotic hallucinatory state. Her growing ability to tolerate separateness helped her develop the capacity for symbolic play and language. After discussing my work with this patient, I go on to elucidate Ogden’s view of the autistic-contiguous position. I suggest that the primordial preverbal interior reactions of the body become the most primal way of signifying reality. On this basis, I develop a set of ideas concerning some intersubjective aspects of autism.

His major fields of interest include children on the autistic spectrum and children of delayed verbal development, as well as early mental states in children and adults.CONTACT Ehud Wolpe ehud.wolpe@gmail.com Israel Psychoanalytic Society, 43 Shalom Aleichem St., Tel Aviv, Israel
Covid-19, child psychoanalysis, e-therapy, crisis management, setting

This paper examines the rapid and dramatic influences that the first wave of the Covid-19 pandemic had on the author’s practice of child psychoanalysis. The author describes the changes in daily routine and the measures that had to be taken to follow regulations and stay ‘on the safe side’, on the one hand, while maintaining the continuity of analyses on the other. This change was rapid and intense, and the main feature of this period was the loss of the ability to withhold action, to stop and think, and to let mental and psychical processes run their course – a feature we are so accustomed to in our usual practice. The consequences of this process are still to be explored, and need more time and perspective for the full impact to be understood. In this paper, the author maps a few issues that will have to be dealt with more fully after the pandemic is over.

Child Psychotherapists’ Fantasies about Working with ‘Cultural Difference’

Anna Fleming

Anna Fleming

London, UK
anna.fleming4@nhs.net

Anna Fleming   Child and adolescent psychotherapist at Islington CAMHS, London, UK, where she works in schools and special schools.
Culture, difference, fantasy, child psychotherapy, psychosocial, cultural difference

Child psychotherapists regularly find themselves working across ‘cultural difference’, yet this reality is given little thought in trainings, be it in supervision, teaching, or in the training analysis. A growing body of literature in the psychotherapy professions emphasises the great anxiety provoked by ‘cultural difference’, and the ensuing defences that are ordinarily employed by individuals; this literature identifies an urgent need for psychotherapists to find more consistently thoughtful ways to engage with issues of race, culture and social class differences. Using Bourdieu’s concept of ‘habitus’ to build a working definition of ‘cultural difference’ and a psychosocial methodology, I interviewed eight child psychotherapists to ask what fantasies about working with ‘cultural difference’ we might hold. Thematic analysis identified two fantasy structures: ‘Difference as Dangerous’, in which ‘cultural difference’ is variously associated with all kinds of badness, including sexual perversion, violence, child abuse, neglect and shame; and ‘the Profession in Peril’, in which it was felt that the child psychotherapy profession is threatened by ‘cultural differences’, both from without and from within. Using discourse analysis, two further fantasies were examined: ‘Neutrality’ in the therapist, in which the therapist is imagined to transcend ‘cultural difference’; and ‘The Location of Difference’, in which it is imagined that one person in a pairing contains all the ‘difference’ and its negative associations, while the other is felt to be ‘normal’. These four fantasies show how powerful projections are able to enter the consulting room. There is an urgent need for the child psychotherapy profession to give thought to ‘cultural difference’, in order to avoid reproducing prejudiced stances; this becomes imperative, as issues of ‘cultural difference’ become more politically explosive.

She worked for fifteen years in an NHS Child and Adolescent Mental Health Service (CAMHS), specialising in Looked After Children, after working as a teacher and SENCo in schools. She practises privately in East Sussex, working with organisations such as Children’s Services, Fostering Agencies and Child and Adolescent Mental Health Trusts, providing therapeutic input, training and consulting. She specialises in children and young people with developmental trauma.CONTACT Angela Evans angela.evans100@gmail.com
Taboo, love, developmental trauma, idealisation, countertransference, loss, fear, containment

This paper explores the taboo of love in the case of children in care. Love can often become a taboo for these children, something they unconsciously forbid themselves from experiencing due to fears of further loss and pain. Love can also become a taboo for the adults working with looked after children, including psychotherapists. The author presents her work with individual looked after children and with the professional network around them. She proposes that love tends not to be a central theme in the care system, despite its relevance to children who have often not experienced adequate love in their early lives. The implication of this proposition is that such children, who may have never known love, or who may have had a distorted experience of love, may be at risk of remaining unloved within the care system, which could seriously compromise their development. The author calls for more support for professionals, so that they can be facilitated to perform their vital work in promoting a loving approach in the system around children in care.

Telehealth, telemedicine, unconscious, transference, parapraxis, Freudian slip, online therapy, Covid-19

As Covid-19 forced psychoanalysts, psychotherapists and many other healthcare practitioners to use online platforms, internet connectivity took on new meaning. While bothersome for both patient and therapist, technology glitches can offer an opportunity to see unconscious relationship dynamics come through in sessions, in a way they might not in the consulting room. While the therapist usually controls the frame through how they arrange their office, internet glitches can come from either the therapist’s or the patient’s side. These glitches can be thought of as either purely technological or as an unconscious enactment, more like a parapraxis. Both kinds of glitches can offer the opportunity to uncover meaning in the relationship. Exploration might help elucidate either the patient’s reaction to the technological glitch or the unconscious meaning behind a parapraxis glitch. Like a ‘Freudian slip’ of the tongue in a typical session, a Freudian glitch can be fertile ground for further examination and connection with patients.

Liz Bodycote

Liz Bodycote

York House
London

Liz Bodycote   liz.bodycote@googlemail.com

If I were asked to name a key text from the days of my training in Child Psychotherapy, it would be Susan Isaacs’s The Nature and Function of Phantasy. Reading this seminal paper for the first time was for me a milestone moment in the development of my understanding of Kleinian theory; its systematic clarity offered me a grasp of the meaning of the idea of unconscious ph-antasy. I was also struck by the explicit setting out of the distinctive character of data gathering in the analytic method; the importance of the observation of context, and the detailed approach that is in the blood of psychoanalytic training, yet here for the first time I saw it set down as a defining ‘method’ of gathering evidence. I learnt that this was one of the Kleinian contributions in the period of ‘The Controversial Discussions’ in the British Psychoanalytical Society in the 1940s, but I otherwise knew nothing of Isaacs as a pioneer. Unlike Winnicott and Bowlby who gained public prominence in the second half of the twentieth century, the contribution of Susan Isaacs in the first half remains relatively unknown.

In Wise words: How Susan Isaacs changed parenting, Caroline Vollans has given us access to Isaacs’s public writings, which appeared under the pseudonym of Ursula Wise between 1929 and 1936. During that time, as an ‘agony aunt’ correspondent in The Nursery World, ‘Ursula Wise’, wrote a weekly parenting column, in which she responded to letters from worried mothers and nannies, describing their dilemmas and difficulties with their young children. Vollans, a primary school teacher for many years, who then trained in psychoanalysis, notes that she came across the work of Isaacs only after her professional trainings, despite Isaacs's influence in the fields of both education and psychoanalysis. Prompted by this gap in recognition, Vollans went on to unearth the Susan Isaacs Archive at the Institute of Education (where Isaacs was head of the Child Development Department in 1933), and has put together a volume of correspondence, which should be of professional, clinical and historical interest for Child Psychotherapists.

Joshua Holmes  

Fred Busch, a Boston-based psychoanalyst, is one of the US analysts who has championed free association, Bionian reverie, and reflection as key psychoanalytic themes. Reverie plays relatively little part in the child psychotherapy literature (but see Hermon, 2016), so here I shall try to draw implications from Busch’s book for our discipline.

While, especially in adult psychoanalysis, there has been a proliferation of interest in reverie in recent times, it is far from clear what people are actually talking about when they refer to reverie. Busch makes a thrust at conceptual clarity by outlining some of the problems and differences in the way the word has been used.

Reverie, from the French word ‘rêve’ – ‘to dream’, in popular usage refers to a daydream-like state. But like many other words, such as ‘projection’, it has become a technical psychoanalytic term.

It is important to situate the emergence of a psychoanalytic reading of reverie in its historical context. Freud had barely written about countertransference publicly and he is generally – though somewhat incorrectly – understood to have viewed countertransference as an unwanted hindrance, and straightforwardly evidence of the need for further analysis for the analyst 264
